concepts.name: Work
concepts.statement: In science, work is not effort but a transfer of energy. A force does work on a system only when the system is displaced and the force has a component along that displacement, and the work is the product of that component and the distance the force acts through, $W = Fd\cos\theta$.

forms.condition: a constant force and one-way motion in one dimension

concepts.name: Sign of the work
concepts.statement: The angle between the force and the displacement decides the sign. The work is positive when the force has a component in the direction of the motion, zero when the force is perpendicular to the motion or when there is no displacement at all, and negative when the force opposes the motion and so removes energy from the system.

concepts.name: Joule
concepts.statement: Work and energy have the units of force times distance, and in SI that is the newton-meter, which is given the name joule. One joule is not a large amount of energy; it would lift a small 100-gram apple a distance of about 1 meter.

concepts.name: Calculating work
concepts.statement: Putting a force, a distance and the angle between them into the definition of work gives the energy the force transfers. Setting the answer beside the energy a person eats in a day gives a feel for the size of a joule.

concepts.name: Energy
concepts.statement: Energy is the ability to do work. Work done on a system transfers energy to it, and work done by a system transfers energy out of it.

concepts.name: Work transfers energy
concepts.statement: Work done on a system puts energy into it, and work done by a system takes energy out of it. Where that energy goes depends on the situation: friction carries it off as heat, while the work done carrying a briefcase up stairs is stored in the briefcase-Earth system and can be recovered at any time.

concepts.name: Net work
concepts.statement: The work that changes a system's motion is the work done by the net external force, and it is also the sum of the work done by each force separately. A force perpendicular to the displacement, such as the weight or the normal force on a package sliding along a belt, does no work and drops out of the sum.

forms.condition: the net force parallel to the displacement

concepts.name: Work as area under a graph
concepts.statement: Plot the component of the force along the motion against the distance and the work is the area beneath the line. That is plain when the force is constant, and it stays true when the force varies, since the area can be cut into strips and each strip is the work done over its own small distance.

concepts.name: Kinetic energy
concepts.statement: The quantity the net work changes is one half the mass times the speed squared, and it is given the name translational kinetic energy: the energy a body has by reason of its motion. Because the speed is squared, a car travelling at 100 km/h carries four times the kinetic energy it carries at 50 km/h, which helps explain why high-speed collisions are so devastating.

concepts.name: Work-energy theorem
concepts.statement: Put Newton's second law and the constant-acceleration relation between speed and distance into the net work and the distance cancels, leaving the net work equal to the change in the kinetic energy. It was derived here for a constant force along the motion, but it holds in general, even for forces that vary in direction and magnitude.

forms.condition: a constant net force parallel to the displacement

concepts.name: Using the work-energy theorem
concepts.statement: Once the net work and the kinetic energies are known, the unknown of a problem can be any one of the three: the final speed, the force that caused the change, or the distance over which it acted. Solutions that go through energy are generally shorter and easier than those that use kinematics and dynamics alone.

concepts.name: Potential energy
concepts.statement: Work done against a force that can give the energy back is not lost; it is stored in the system as potential energy. Potential energy is a property of a system rather than of a single body, since it belongs to the arrangement of the parts: lifting a mass stores energy in the mass-Earth system, and the system gives it back when the mass comes down.

concepts.name: Gravitational potential energy
concepts.statement: Lifting a mass at constant speed takes a force equal to its weight, so the work done in raising it through a height is the weight times the height. That work is the change in the gravitational potential energy of the object-Earth system, and it is the same whether the mass is lifted or lowered, with the sign of the height carrying the difference.

forms.condition: a change in height h that is small compared with the radius of Earth
an object lifted straight up at constant speed

concepts.name: Reference level for potential energy
concepts.statement: Gravitational potential energy depends on relative position, so a level has to be chosen at which it is called zero. Earth's surface is the usual choice, but the choice is arbitrary: what relates to the work done, and so what has physical significance, is the difference between two positions. The rise between the first two rungs of a ladder is worth the same as the rise between the last two.

concepts.name: Path independence of work against gravity
concepts.statement: The change in gravitational potential energy is the weight times the change in height for any path between two points, not only for a straight lift, as long as the height change is small compared with the radius of Earth. Multiplying mass, gravity and height therefore replaces working out the work done along a complicated path.

concepts.name: Potential energy into kinetic energy
concepts.statement: Release a raised mass and gravity does work equal to the potential energy given up, so the kinetic energy grows by exactly that amount. When friction is negligible, the speed of a falling body then depends only on its initial speed and on the change in height, and not on its mass or on the path it takes.

forms.condition: work done by frictional forces is negligible
work done by frictional forces is negligible

concepts.name: Finding a stopping force
concepts.statement: A body that lands has kinetic energy that must be taken away by the work the ground does on it, and that work is the stopping force times the distance the body travels while stopping. Because the distance sits in the denominator, stopping in half a centimetre takes a force hundreds of times the body's weight, and bending the legs to stop over half a metre cuts that force a hundredfold.

concepts.name: Conservative force
concepts.statement: A conservative force is one for which the work done by it or against it depends only on where the motion starts and where it ends, and not on the path between. Gravity is one and the force of an ideal spring is another, and it is exactly this property that lets a potential energy be defined for the force, so that the work need never be calculated along the path at all.

concepts.name: Potential energy of a spring
concepts.statement: The force needed to stretch a spring grows from zero to the force constant times the stretch, so its average is half of that, and the work done is one half the force constant times the stretch squared. The same quantity is the area of the triangle under the graph of force against stretch, and because the spring force is conservative that work is stored and can be fully recovered.

forms.condition: Hooke's law applies to the spring
Hooke's law applies to the spring

concepts.name: Mechanical energy
concepts.statement: The total kinetic plus potential energy of a system is called its mechanical energy. Writing it as one quantity is what lets a problem be answered by comparing two configurations, since in a system with only conservative forces the energy changes only in form, moving between kinetic energy and the various kinds of potential energy while the total stays put.

concepts.name: Conservation of mechanical energy
concepts.statement: If only conservative forces act, the work-energy theorem says the change in kinetic energy is the work done by those forces, and that work is minus the change in potential energy. The two changes therefore cancel, so the kinetic and potential energies of the system add to a constant and the values at the start equal the values at the end.

forms.condition: conservative forces only, a gravitational force and a spring

concepts.name: Using conservation of mechanical energy
concepts.statement: The way to use conservation of mechanical energy is to write every kind of energy the system has at the start and at the end, strike out the terms that are zero by choosing the heights and the moments well, and solve for the one that is left. The details of the path in between never enter, which is what makes the method so much shorter than following the forces.

concepts.name: Nonconservative force
concepts.statement: A nonconservative force is one for which the work done depends on the path taken, and friction is the plain example: the longer the route between two points, the more work is done against it. Because the work depends on the path, no potential energy can be defined for such a force, and the work it does has to be counted directly.

concepts.name: Dissipation by friction
concepts.statement: The work done by a nonconservative force adds mechanical energy to a system or removes it. Friction removes it: the energy becomes thermal energy that spreads out and leaves the system, and even where the thermal energy is caught and kept it cannot be fully turned back into work, so it is lost in that sense as well.

concepts.name: Work by nonconservative forces
concepts.statement: Split the net work into the part done by conservative forces and the part done by nonconservative ones, and replace the conservative part by minus the change in potential energy. What is left says that the total mechanical energy changes by exactly the work the nonconservative forces do: positive work adds to it, negative work takes from it, and zero work leaves it conserved.

concepts.name: Solving an energy problem with friction
concepts.statement: With friction in the problem, the work it does is the friction force times the distance, taken as negative because it opposes the motion, and it goes into the energy equation beside the kinetic and potential energies. Solving for the distance or the final speed then takes one line, where following the forces would mean combining the weight, the normal force and friction as vectors first.

concepts.name: Law of conservation of energy
concepts.statement: Total energy is constant in any process. It may change in form or pass from one system to another, but the total remains the same, and writing the law down means adding to the mechanical energy and the nonconservative work one more term for every other kind of energy the system holds. In most problems all but a few of those terms are the same at the start and at the end and simply cancel.

concepts.name: Forms of energy
concepts.statement: Energy takes many forms besides the mechanical ones. Electrical energy travels with a flow of charge, chemical energy sits in the bonds of a fuel or a food, and radiant energy travels in electromagnetic waves. Nuclear energy comes from changes inside a nucleus, and thermal energy lies in the random motion of atoms and molecules. Each can turn into any other, and each can do work.

concepts.name: Transformation of energy
concepts.statement: The changing of energy from one form into others is happening all the time, and most chains run through several forms: the chemical energy in coal becomes thermal energy in steam, which becomes the mechanical energy of a spinning turbine, which becomes electrical energy. Sunlight on a solar cell becomes electricity and then the motion of a motor.

concepts.name: Efficiency
concepts.statement: Energy is conserved in a conversion, but the useful energy or work that comes out is always less than the energy put in, and the efficiency is the ratio of the two. A coal-fired power plant turns about 40 percent of the chemical energy in its fuel into electricity, and the rest leaves as thermal energy through the flue and the cooling towers.

concepts.name: Solving an energy problem
concepts.statement: The strategy has six steps. Settle the system and what the problem asks. Look at every force and ask whether you know its potential energy. Use conservation of mechanical energy where every force is conservative and the general law where one is not. Strike out the zero terms before doing any algebra. Then check that the signs and the size of the answer are reasonable.

concepts.name: Electrical energy
concepts.statement: Electrical energy is the energy carried by a flow of charge.

concepts.name: Chemical energy
concepts.statement: Chemical energy is the energy in a substance stored in the bonds between atoms and molecules, which can be released in a chemical reaction.

concepts.name: Radiant energy
concepts.statement: Radiant energy is the energy carried by electromagnetic waves.

concepts.name: Nuclear energy
concepts.statement: Nuclear energy is energy released by changes within atomic nuclei, such as the fusion of two light nuclei or the fission of a heavy one.

concepts.name: Thermal energy
concepts.statement: Thermal energy is the energy within an object due to the random motion of its atoms and molecules, and it accounts for the object's temperature.

concepts.name: Power
concepts.statement: Power is the rate at which work is done, and since work is a transfer of energy it is also the rate at which energy is spent. A 60-W light bulb spends 60 J every second. Great power means a large amount of work done or energy spent in a short time, which is what a dragster, a volcano and a rocket have in common.

concepts.name: Watt
concepts.statement: The SI unit of power is the watt, one joule per second. The older horsepower is still used for motors and engines, and one horsepower is 746 watts, so the woman running up the stairs puts out a little less than a horsepower; a person can beat that for a few seconds, and a horse can hold it for hours.

concepts.name: Calculating power
concepts.statement: Finding a power output means first finding all the work or the energy that went into the job, kinetic and gravitational alike, and then dividing by the time it took. Doing it once shows where the effort really goes: of the woman's 538 W, climbing takes almost all of it and speeding up takes barely a fifteenth.

concepts.name: Energy from power
concepts.statement: Turn the definition of power around and the energy a device uses is its power times the time it runs. Electricity bills are written in kilowatt-hours, the product of a power in kilowatts and a time in hours, because household appliances draw about a kilowatt for hours at a stretch and that makes the number a convenient size.

concepts.name: Estimating the cost of energy
concepts.statement: The cost of running something is its power times the time it runs times the price of a kilowatt-hour, so it is high only when both the power and the hours are high. That is why it pays to go after water heaters and air conditioners rather than toasters, which draw a great deal for a few minutes, or electric clocks, which draw almost nothing all day.

concepts.name: Kilowatt-hour
concepts.statement: The kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, the energy used in one hour at a power of one kilowatt, and it is the unit in which electric utility companies bill electrical energy.

concepts.name: Horsepower
concepts.statement: The horsepower is an older non-SI unit of power, with one horsepower equal to 746 watts.

concepts.name: Body as an energy converter
concepts.statement: Our own bodies are energy conversion machines, and conservation of energy applies to them as it does to anything else: the chemical energy stored in food becomes work, thermal energy, or chemical energy stored in fatty tissue. How much goes to each depends on how much is eaten and on how active the person is, and anything eaten beyond what is needed goes to fat.

concepts.name: Metabolic rate
concepts.statement: The rate at which the body uses food energy to stay alive and to do things is its metabolic rate, a power like any other. The rate at rest is the basal metabolic rate, about 85 W, and it is divided among the organs, with the liver and spleen taking the largest share and the brain the next. About 75 percent of the calories burned in a day go to these basic functions.

concepts.name: Oxygen consumption and energy use
concepts.statement: Digestion is the oxidation of food, so the energy a person spends is directly proportional to the oxygen they take in: about 20 kJ of energy for each litre of oxygen consumed, whatever the food. You can therefore measure a person's power output simply by measuring their breathing.

concepts.name: Useful work
concepts.statement: Work done by a person means work done on the outside world, such as lifting weights, climbing stairs or accelerating to a run. Internal work, such as the heart pumping blood or the muscles of a shiver pulling against one another, is not counted, even though it costs energy; the forces the body exerts are nonconservative, so they can change the mechanical energy of whatever is worked on.

concepts.name: Finding the efficiency of an activity
concepts.statement: A person's efficiency is the useful work they do divided by the food energy they metabolise doing it, and for most activities it is small: a fifth at best for cycling and climbing, a fiftieth for swimming at the surface. Knowing the rate from the table and the useful work from the physics gives the ratio, and it explains why exercise burns so much food for so little lifted.

concepts.name: Basal metabolic rate
concepts.statement: The basal metabolic rate is the total energy conversion rate of a person at rest.

concepts.name: Renewable energy sources
concepts.statement: Renewable forms of energy are those that cannot be used up: water, wind, solar and biomass. They are still a small share of the world's supply, but they are the fastest growing part of it, and some countries already draw a large fraction of their electricity from them, as New Zealand does from hydroelectric power.

concepts.name: Fossil fuels
concepts.statement: About 85 percent of the world's energy comes from the nonrenewable fossil fuels, oil, natural gas and coal, and roughly a third of it from oil alone, much of that for transport. Demand has tripled in the past fifty years and may triple again in the next thirty, and the likelihood of a link between fossil fuel use and global warming has made the shift away from them urgent.

concepts.name: Energy use and economic well-being
concepts.statement: In most countries a higher standard of living, measured as gross domestic product per capita, comes with a higher energy use per capita, so access to reliable energy is a condition of economic growth. Diversifying the sources changes that dependency and makes a grid quicker to bring back after a storm or a conflict, which the last twenty years of disruptions have shown.

concepts.name: Degradation of energy
concepts.statement: The law of conservation of energy says the total in an isolated system never changes; the philosophy of energy conservation is about using less of it. The two do not conflict. Most energy transformations end in degraded waste heat: the total is still there, but its potential to do useful work has gone. That is why resources run out even though energy does not.
